x: Hermione is a project workspace that lives on your Mac. Issues, a kanban board, a backlog, sprints, a roadmap, releases and a handbook of pages, in one window, saved to one file you own. There is no account, no server and no subscription to use it. It is free and open source under Apache 2.0. Press ⌘J and say what you want, "create a bug for @priya due friday" or "plan the next sprint with 20 points", and Hermione makes the change, shows you the plan first when there's more than one step, and lets you undo it. A small model trained for exactly this job can run on your Mac to understand more; i

One person running a real project. A thesis, a side project, a freelance client, a product you're building alone, tracked with the same tools a team would use, without signing up for one. Small teams that want their plan on their own machines. Sync between devices is being built (end to end encrypted, through a relay you can host yourself); today each workspace lives on one Mac. Anyone who wants AI help without sending their work to a cloud. The assistant works offline. The optional model runs locally.

Hermione rebuilds the familiar shapes of tools like Jira and Confluence, in its own original code. It is not affiliated with Atlassian; those names are theirs.
Hermione runs on Apple silicon Macs (M1 or later) with macOS 11 Big Sur or later. Intel Macs can build it from source. A Windows build is produced in CI but not yet published.

1. Download Hermione 0.3.0 aarch64.dmg (about 20 MB) from the latest release. 2. Open the DMG and drag Hermione into Applications . 3. The first time, right click Hermione → Open , then Open again. The app is not yet signed with an Apple Developer ID, so macOS asks before opening it the first time. After that it opens like any other app. If macOS says it "is damaged and can't be opened", that is the same check being stricter about a downloaded file; run this once and open it again: 4. Hermione asks your name, what you do and how it should look, then opens.
Everything is saved to one folder: You can move it anywhere, a synced folder for example, in Settings → Your data → Data folder . More in Your data.

Choose Hermione → Check for Updates (or Settings → About ). Hermione asks GitHub for the latest release, sending only its version number, and tells you if there's a newer one. Download it and drag it over the old copy; your data is kept. Every version reads every older data format; this is tested on each change with saved data from every past version. After an update, What's new shows once with the changes.
Drag Hermione from Applications to the Trash. Your data stays in its folder until you delete that too: If you downloaded Hermione AI, the model files are in the same folder (about 1.3 GB each).

For development, or to use Hermione in a browser tab. You need Node 20.9 or later, pnpm 12, and, for the desktop app, Rust (stable) and the Xcode command line tools. The desktop build downloads a pinned llama.cpp release once and bundles its llama server ; set HERMIONE SKIP LLAMA=1 to build without it. The browser version is the same interface with the data in IndexedDB. Use Settings → Your data → Export → Everything (JSON) to keep a copy, and Restore from an export to move it into the Mac app.

G then B . The active sprint, one column per status in your workflow. Drag a card to another column or another place in its column. The toast that follows has Undo , and ⌘Z works too. Drag from the keyboard: focus a card, press Space to pick it up, the arrow keys to move it, Space to drop it, Esc to put it back. Click a card to open it in a side panel. ⌘ click opens the full issue. Add issue at the foot of a column creates one already in that status. Shift click or ⌘ click cards, or press X on a focused card, to select more than one. A bar appears: move, assign, set the priority, or move them all to the Trash. Drag one selected card and the rest come with it.
Right click any card (or press Shift+F10 on it) for its status, priority, assign to me, copy key, copy link, archive and Trash.

G then L . Everything not in a running sprint, ranked. Drag rows to change the order; the top is what you'd do next. Drag issues into a planned sprint at the top of the page, or select several and pick a sprint.

G then S . Plan a sprint, start it, finish it. 1. Create a sprint with a name, a goal and a length (one to six weeks). 2. Fill it by dragging issues in from the backlog. The header adds up the points as you go, against your average velocity from past sprints. 3. Start sprint. Its issues appear on the board. 4. During the sprint, the burndown shows the points left against an even line to zero, and the ring in the board header shows points done. 5. Complete sprint. Choose where unfinished issues go: the backlog or the next sprint. Hermione keeps a sprint report : what was finished, what was carr
G then R . Epics on a timeline. Drag a bar to move it, drag its ends to change its start or end. Each bar fills in as its child issues are done.

G then E . Group the issues that ship together under a version, see how many are done, and mark it released on the day. The assistant can write the release notes from those issues: "draft release notes".
G then C . A month with every issue on its due date. Move between months, or jump back with Today .
G then W . Open points per person, so you can see who has too much before you plan the next sprint. Click a person to see their issues.

New issues from quick capture and imports land in Triage first. Move through them with J and K , then: Key Does A Accept into the backlog M Assign to me and accept S Snooze for a week D Decline and archive Nothing in triage counts toward sprints or reports until it's accepted.

Each project has its own key ( WEB , APP ) that prefixes its issues ( WEB 12 ), its own workflow, people, labels and fields. Switch projects from the card at the top of the sidebar, or start one with New project . All projects , in the same menu, shows every project's open and overdue issues and sprint progress on one page. Give a project an icon and a colour in Settings → Project . Archive a project you've finished; it stays searchable and can be restored.
An issue is one piece of work: a bug, a task, a story, an epic that holds others, or a subtask. Its key, like HER 12 , is the project key plus a number, and stays the same forever.

Press C anywhere, or New issue on Home. Add issue at the foot of a board column. ⌘J and say it: "create a bug: login fails on Safari, high priority, for @priya, due friday". ⇧⌘Space from any app on your Mac opens quick capture. From a page: a to do line in a description can become a child issue with one click. Issue templates (Bug, Feature, Chore) fill the description with the usual headings.

Markdown, @mentions (the person sees it in their Inbox), files, and reactions on any comment. Vote on an issue to show it matters. Watch an issue to hear about every change.

Pages are the handbook beside the work: specs, meeting notes, runbooks, decisions. G then P .

The editor is Markdown with a toolbar, so headings, lists, to dos, tables, quotes, code, links and images all work the way you'd type them. Type / at the start of a line for a menu of blocks: heading, subheading, bulleted, numbered and to do lists, quote, code block, table, divider, image, diagram and a live issue list. Type @ to mention a person, or an issue key like HER 4 to link it. ⌘B , ⌘I and ⌘K for bold, italic and a link. ⌘↵ saves. Paste or drop a file or image to attach it. A table of contents appears beside long pages.

Every editor has three tabs: Write (the Markdown), Visual and Preview . Visual shows the page formatted; click a block to edit just that block's Markdown in place, with the toolbar, the / menu and mentions all working.
New page offers templates: meeting notes, a decision record, a retrospective, a project brief and a how to guide. Save as template on any page adds it to the gallery; your own templates show first.

A code block marked mermaid is drawn as a diagram, in your theme, by Hermione's own parser and layout. Flowcharts and sequence diagrams are drawn; other kinds stay as text. Linked from at the foot of a page lists the issues, pages and comments that mention it.
History keeps every saved version. Pick two to compare them side by side with changes marked, and restore any version (the current one is kept too).
Select any text to comment on that passage. Comments on the whole page sit at the bottom. Both support @mentions.
Drag pages in the tree to reorder them or nest one under another. Labels on pages filter the list; Private makes a page only you can see. Give a page an icon and a cover .
Export saves a page as a Markdown file, or prints it ( Save as PDF in the Mac print dialog). To export every page at once, see Your data.
G then H . What needs you today: your open issues, what's due this week, recently edited pages, the running sprint, and the project's shape by status, type, priority and person.

G then D . A short list you pick each morning. Add issues from the suggestions (due soon, in progress, assigned to you), drag them into the order you'll do them, and tick them off. It keeps until tomorrow.
G then N . Mentions of you, comments on issues you watch, and work assigned to you, newest first. The red count in the sidebar is what you haven't read.

⌘K (or / ) searches every issue, page and comment, and every command. Type an issue key ( HER 12 ), words from a title or a description, or a person's name. Filter the results to Issues , Pages or Views with the chips at the top. Commands are searchable by what they do: "dark", "density", "new sprint", "export". Settings are too: "licence" opens Settings → Plan . What you've opened recently shows first when the box is empty.

Issues and pages show up in macOS Spotlight ( ⌘Space ) by key and title, kept current as you work. Choosing one opens it in Hermione. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy ; that also removes everything Hermione added to the index.

⇧⌘Space from any app opens a small Hermione window. Type an issue in one line with shorthand, press Return , and it lands in Triage without leaving what you were doing: Shorthand Sets bug: task: story: epic: at the start The type p1 … p4 , or !!! !! The priority ( p1 is highest) @noah , @me The assignee web A label 3pts , 3 points The estimate today , friday , next week , in 3 days , dec 3 The due date Whatever is left becomes the summary. The same shorthand works in Add issue on the board and in ⌘K.

The Mac app reminds you about issues due today or late: once shortly after it opens, then every hour, never more than once a day for the same issue. Daily digest (off until you turn it on, Settings → You ): once a day after the hour you choose, one notification with what's due, what's late, what's unread and what's left in the sprint. It's worked out on your Mac; a day with nothing to say is skipped.

Name, description, icon and colour. The key prefixes every issue and can only change while the project has no issues. Archive project hides it from the switcher; Restore brings it back.

The statuses that become board columns, in order. Each belongs to a category, To do , In progress or Done , which decides what counts as started and finished in progress bars and reports. Rename, reorder, add or remove them; removing one asks where its issues should go.

Click Rules on a status to decide: Which statuses an issue can come from. For example, Done only from In review . What it needs before it moves in: an assignee, points, a due date, a description or a time estimate. A move that breaks a rule is refused with the reason, on the board, in lists and from the assistant alike.

Rules that do the busywork. Each has a when and a then : When Then An issue is created Set its priority An issue moves into a status Assign it to someone Add a label Move it to a status Add it to the current sprint Close its child issues For example: when an issue moves into Done, close its child issues , or when a bug is created, add it to the current sprint . Rules don't set each other off, and a rule that can't apply to an issue is skipped without blocking the change.
Everyone who can be assigned work or mentioned: a name, a handle for @mentions, and an email if you like. Hermione runs on your Mac, so these are names, not accounts.
Labels have colours that show on cards; renaming one changes it on every issue. Custom fields add text, number, choice or date fields to every issue's Details panel.

Chores that come back: give a summary, how often (every day, every weekday, every week, every two weeks or every month), the first day and an assignee. Each is created on its day, the next time the project is open, due that day.

Which engine answers ⌘J : the built in one only, Hermione AI (Pro), or your own model server. Also the web settings for Hermione AI + Web, and Recent actions , a log of what the assistant did. See The assistant and Hermione AI models.

Everything that can ever leave this Mac, listed in full: when, where to, and what's sent. Your projects, issues and pages never leave. The assistant never does either, with the built in engine or Hermione AI. Web answers send only the search words; update checks send only the version, and only when you ask. Here too: the Show in Spotlight switch. Hermione has no account, no analytics and no tracking. See Privacy and security.
The version, the data folder, the bundled llama.cpp runtime, and Copy diagnostics : a short report for bug reports with versions and counts, and none of your project text.
Everything you make in Hermione is saved on your Mac, in files you can see, copy and back up. Nothing depends on a server or a plan.

Every change is saved at once, written to a temporary file first and then swapped in, so a crash or a full disk never leaves half a file. The browser version keeps the same data in the browser's IndexedDB. Settings → Your data → Data folder moves everything to another folder, a synced one or an external drive, and the app follows it.

The first save each day copies the previous day's file into backups/ ; the newest 14 are kept. Settings → Your data → Backups lists them; Restore replaces the workspace with one (the current state is backed up first, so a restore can itself be undone).
⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z undo and redo any change, including the assistant's. ⇧⌘H shows the last 30 changes in words and jumps back to any of them. See Undo history.
Deleted issues and pages wait in Settings → Trash for 30 days, then go for good. Restore puts one back where it was, with its comments and history. Delete for good skips the wait.

When one request would change more than five things, or a model proposes more than one change, Hermione shows the plan first: every step in words, each with a tick box. Untick what you don't want, then Apply , or Cancel . Some things always ask first, whatever their size: archiving issues and completing a sprint. One request can never change more than 25 things.

Every answer that changed something has Undo this (or Undo these 6 changes ), and everything the assistant does also goes into the normal undo history ( ⌘Z , ⇧⌘H ) and each issue's History . Fields the assistant set carry a small mark with the sentence that set them.

The assistant has two engines, and uses them in order. 1. The built in engine reads common sentences with hand written rules: issue keys, statuses by meaning ("finished", "shipped", "wip"), priorities ("p1", "urgent", "blocker"), people ("me", "@noah", "Priya"), dates ("friday", "end of the week", "in 3 days", "dec 3"), points, labels and sprints. It answers in milliseconds, offline, with no model at all. This is what you get by default. 2. A model , if one is set up, for anything the engine can't place: vague requests, long sentences with several things in them, questions. It sees the same to

It says so, with examples of what it can do. Rephrase with an issue key and a plain verb ("move HER 3 to done"), or set up Hermione AI or your own model for looser language.

Hermione AI is a small language model trained to do one job: turn what you type in ⌘J into Hermione's own tool calls. It runs on your Mac with llama.cpp on the Apple silicon GPU. Nothing you type goes anywhere. Hermione AI 2B Hermione AI + Web 2B For Everything in your workspace, offline The same, plus looking things up online Exact match on 500 unseen requests 92.6% 91.2% Right tools, any arguments 97.2% 96.2% Base model Qwen3.5 2B Qwen3.5 2B Download 1.32 GB, 4 bit 1.32 GB, 4 bit Memory while running about 2 GB about 2 GB Licence Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Both are on Hugging Face at ansarbuilds/

The test is strict. 500 requests the model never saw in training, in projects with different people, workflows and issue keys. A request counts only if the model makes exactly the right calls with exactly the right arguments, the right issue keys, the right status name, the right date. Fine tuning took the base model from 47.2% to 92.6% exact. The biggest gains are where a general model doesn't know Hermione's conventions: creating issues (4 of 70 right before, 61 after), writing pages (1 of 14 → 14 of 14), moving issues into sprints (1 → 13 of 14), several requests in one sentence (3 → 16 of

1. Settings → Plan: activate Hermione Pro (see Pro). 2. Settings → Assistant → Hermione AI → Download model. The download can be paused and resumed. When it finishes, Hermione: 1. checks the list of models it downloaded from GitHub is signed with Hermione's Ed25519 key, whose public half is built into the app; 2. checks the file's SHA 256 against that signed list, and refuses it if they differ; 3. starts the llama server that ships inside the app, on 127.0.0.1 only, on a free port, with an 8,192 token context, and stops it when it's not needed. A model that's too big for your Mac's memory is m

The files are Apache 2.0. You can run them in any llama.cpp based app (Ollama, LM Studio) and point Hermione at it under Settings → Assistant → Your model , which is free: Then the address http://127.0.0.1:8080 , Test connection , Save .

For each request: the instructions ( packages/core/src/assistant/prompt.ts ), the tool list, and a plain text description of the project built by contextFor in packages/core/src/assistant/execute.ts : today's date, who you are, the issue on screen, the statuses, people and sprints, and one line per issue (up to 150) with its key, summary, status, priority, assignee, points and type. Then the last eight turns of the conversation and your sentence. It never leaves your Mac. It answers with tool calls, which Hermione checks against the workflow's rules and the limits before anything changes.

A 4B model (from Qwen3 4B Instruct 2507) was trained the same way and scored 74.8%, under the 85% release gate, so it wasn't published. Most of its misses were answers that were right but came back in a shape the server didn't turn into tool calls (Qwen3 4B writes <tool call blocks its chat template doesn't round trip), so the next step is fixing how it's served, not more training.

It knows Hermione's tools and nothing else well. Outside them it's a 2B model. English only, for now. It doesn't remember past conversations beyond the last few turns. It can be wrong. Plans, confirmations and undo are there for that.

Everything used to train Hermione AI is in the repository's ml/ folder: the data generator, the training script, the evaluation, the export, and a one command script for a rented GPU. You can retrain it, try another base model, or teach it your own way of working.

generate dataset.py needs no packages and no network, and is deterministic with seed . Each example is a made up project (people, a workflow, sprints, 8 to 30 issues), a request written the way people type, and the exact tool calls that carry it out. It covers 26 kinds of request: creating, moving, assigning, follow ups ("and make it urgent"), corrections ("oops, I meant in progress"), several requests in one sentence, vague requests that should get a question back, and plain chat that needs no tool at all. The last two matter: small models fine tuned on tools tend to forget when not to call o
Uses Apple's MLX. Close other apps on an 8 GB Mac. The full guide, with presets and timings: training on a Mac.

Hermione is one TypeScript and Rust monorepo: about 32,000 lines of TypeScript and 18,000 of Rust. The interface is React, the rules live in a shared TypeScript core, and the Mac app is a Tauri 2 shell in Rust that stores the data, runs the model and talks to macOS.

The Mac app bundles llama.cpp's llama server (build b12823 , pinned in apps/desktop/scripts/llama.json ) and only the libraries it links. When the assistant needs the model, models.rs starts it on 127.0.0.1 on a free port with jinja c 8192 no webui , waits for it to load, and stops it when it's done. Models are listed in a models.json signed with Ed25519; the app checks the signature with public keys compiled into both the Rust shell and the TypeScript core (a test fails if they differ), then checks each file's SHA 256.

A workspace is one JSON document per data folder holding every project, plus attachments as files. Every older format opens unchanged: packages/core/fixtures/upgrade holds data folders written by each past version's own code, and a test opens every one with the core, the file store and the Rust store on each change.

crates/hermione sync maps the workspace onto Automerge documents, so two devices can change the same project offline and merge without conflicts. crates/hermione relay is the relay: it stores and forwards changes that are encrypted on the device, so it sees only their size and timing. It's built and tested but not switched on in the app yet.
The reasoning behind the big choices is in docs/decisions/ : the stack, an independent implementation (no code from any other product), moving the rules into one core, and the sync design.

h: How the app is locked down
x: The window can do very little. The Mac app's windows get only Tauri's core permissions: no shell, no general file access, no arbitrary network. Each thing the interface needs (save, read an attachment, start the model) is one narrowly checked Rust command. A strict content policy. Scripts load only from the app itself; there is no remote code. Web links open in your browser, not in Hermione's window. Markdown never becomes HTML. Pages and comments are parsed into interface elements, so a page can't run a script. Names and paths are checked. Store names can't contain .. or slashes, attachment i

The list of models is signed with Ed25519 using a key that is kept offline, never on a build machine. The app checks the signature against public keys built into it; an unsigned or altered list is refused. Each model file is checked against the SHA 256 in that signed list before it loads. A mismatch deletes the file. Pro licence keys are signed the same way and checked on your Mac, with no account and no network call.
Please report security issues privately, as described in SECURITY.md , not in a public issue.

Hermione is free and open source, and every feature in the app is free forever. Hermione Pro (CA$10 a month or CA$100 a year) pays for the things that cost money to make and run, and adds them on top. Online checkout is being set up. Until it opens, Get Pro in Settings → Plan leads here; get in touch through ansarbuilds.dev for a key.

A licence is a signed key that looks like HERMIONE eyJ2Ijox….Fh3k… . 1. Settings → Plan → Have a licence key? Paste it and press Activate . 2. Hermione checks the key's signature on your Mac. No account, no internet, nothing sent anywhere. 3. Pro features switch on. Each key has an end date: monthly plans get a fresh key each month, yearly plans each year. If a renewal is late, Pro keeps working for 14 more days .

Your data is never held hostage. If Pro ends, every project, page and backup stays and keeps working. Only the Pro features switch off. Never paywalled: your data, export, import, backups, the full app, working offline, using your own model, and building Hermione from source. Still open source. All the code, including the Pro features, is Apache 2.0. Anyone may build their own copy. What Pro buys is the trained models delivered and kept up to date, the hosted services, and the people behind them. The name and logo are trademarks; forks should use their own.

h: Why charge for an open-source app?
x: GPU time to train the models, hosting the downloads, a search relay, the sync relay, Apple's developer fee for signed builds, and the time to build all of it. It's the same deal as Obsidian Sync or Zed Pro.

Is it really free? Yes. Every feature in the app is free and stays free, and the code is Apache 2.0. Pro adds the one click trained model, web answers and (soon) sync. Does it need the internet? No. Everything works offline, including the assistant. The internet is used only for things you ask for: downloading a model, web answers, checking for updates. Can my team use it? Each workspace lives on one Mac today, and the people in it are names for assigning and mentioning, not accounts. Sync between devices is built and being switched on next. Is it a Jira clone?
